lines: Katalyst turns a plain-language intent into a verified settlement on Portaldot.
Today I will run one for real, live on the Portaldot V3 testnet.
Intent in, settlement out.
You say what you want. GenLayer validators agree on the route. A vault on Portaldot checks that route and pays the pools.
The figures on this page are read straight from the vault's events on Portaldot.
In the app, I describe my intent: maximize yield, but only A-Tier carbon pools.
Before depositing anything, I can ask the validators for a free preview.
Two pools qualify, and the lower rated pool is excluded, with the reason shown.
I lock the route, so the vault pays exactly this route or nothing, and deposit three tenths of a testnet POT.
This is a real transaction, signed and sent to Portaldot.
Now GenLayer's validators reach consensus. Most of them agree.
The relayer proposes the route to the vault, but cannot move funds yet.
A safety delay starts. The vault owner can veto during it, and a guardian checks the route against the validators' verdict.
When the delay ends, the vault settles on Portaldot.
Here is that settlement block in Portaldot's own explorer.
It is a real Ethereum style transaction, executed on the Portaldot testnet and sent to our vault contract.
Now the part that matters most. Do not trust us, verify.
This page rebuilds the story from Portaldot events and the validators' own records: the deposit, the consensus, the route that was paid, the fee, the route lock and the safety delay.
Every check passes.
We also tested a failure on testnet. A relayer proposed a route the validators never chose.
The guardian caught it during the delay, the owner vetoed it, and the depositor got every token back.
Verify marks it: the safety delay caught a bad route.
The vault's rules, its fee, cap, timeout and delay, are fixed at deployment. Nobody can change them.
Katalyst. GenLayer decides, Portaldot settles, and anyone can verify.
It is live on testnet today and open source. Next come an audit, a relayer quorum, and mainnet.
